methodological_rigor.justification: The study applies a previously developed and validated XGBoost-based insulin resistance prediction model (AI-IR) to the UK Biobank (~370,000 cancer-free participants) using prospectively linked NHS records. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age and sex (and additionally BMI) are appropriate for incident cancer outcomes, with age-as-time-scale sensitivity analyses addressing age confounding. Bonferroni correction (0.05/43 = 1.163×10^-3) is applied for multiple cancer testing, and joint/interaction analyses with smoking and established metrics are performed. Limitations include the model was originally trained on fasted samples while UK Biobank was not consistently fasted (addressed via fasting-duration sensitivity), self-reported race used as model input, and no causal inference (no Mendelian randomization in this work).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Demonstrating that a clinically derivable AI-IR score predicts incidence of six cancer types after Bonferroni correction has tangible population-health implications for risk stratification and targeted screening. Effect sizes are modest (HRs ~1.14-2.34 for specific cancers; composite HR 1.25) but the scale (UK Biobank) and use of routinely available inputs (BMI, FPG, HbA1c, lipids) make it deployable. This is a prospective cohort analysis applying a prediction model, Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical utility for screening pathways is plausible but not yet validated prospectively.

reporting_quality.justification: The study reports a predictive model applied to an external prospective cohort, for which TRIPOD is most applicable. Methods clearly describe data sources (UK Biobank ID 78912), cohort inclusion, outcome ascertainment (ICD-10 codes from NHS records, specific Data-Fields), model inputs, censoring dates, and statistical approaches. A Source Data file is mentioned for each figure and a Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary is referenced. Key gaps include no explicit TRIPOD checklist citation, no calibration or decision-curve analysis for cancer outcomes, and limited detail on handling of missing clinical parameters when computing AI-IR in UK Biobank.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is applying a specific machine-learning insulin-resistance score (AI-IR) at UK Biobank scale to systematically examine associations with ~43 cancer types, providing BMI-dependent and -independent effect decomposition. While the link between insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia/obesity and several cancers is previously established (cited Mendelian randomization and observational studies), the use of an ML surrogate outperforming MetS/BMI/TyG/TG-HDL as a single integrated metric, and the systematic cancer-type breakdown with Bonferroni correction, is a meaningful incremental contribution. The AI-IR model itself was published previously (ref 23); this work is an application to a new outcome.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well structured with a clear research question, methodical progression from diabetes prediction through cancer incidence and BMI dependence, and a balanced discussion that explicitly acknowledges limitations (Caucasian-predominant cohort, lack of mechanistic link, potential model improvements). Figures are logically organized and Source Data is provided. The writing is clear throughout; minor issues include some repetitive phrasing between Results and Discussion.

key_strengths: Large prospective cohort (UK Biobank, ~370,000 cancer-free participants) with NHS-linked incident cancer outcomes
Systematic evaluation across 43 cancer types with Bonferroni correction; six cancers significantly increased with AI-IR
Head-to-head comparison showing AI-IR outperforms BMI, MetS, TG/HDL, and TyG for diabetes prediction and matches or exceeds for composite cancer
BMI-adjusted analyses identify BMI-independent lung cancer association, adding mechanistic nuance
Age-as-time-scale sensitivity analyses robustly control for age confounding
Source data provided for all figures and approved UK Biobank research ID (78912)
key_concerns: Effect sizes are modest (composite HR 1.25 adjusted for age/sex, 1.16 after BMI adjustment) and clinical actionability for screening is not yet demonstrated
UK Biobank is predominantly European ancestry aged 40-69 and has known healthy-volunteer bias, limiting generalizability
Blood samples not consistently fasted while the AI-IR model was trained on fasting values; sensitivity analyses partially but not fully resolve this
Race is a model input based on self-report, with ethical and generalizability implications that are briefly acknowledged but not deeply explored
No mechanistic or causal inference (no Mendelian randomization extension here); association not causation
TRIPOD not explicitly cited; no calibration or decision-curve analysis for cancer outcomes
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, adequately reported UK Biobank epidemiology paper with a meaningful but incremental finding; tier 2 (e.g., Nature Communications, EClinicalMedicine scope) is defensible with minor revisions to reporting.
